text: The Celts lived across much of Europe, from Spain and Ireland to the river Danube.
Their story begins about 2,800 years ago, when people in central Europe learned to work iron.
src: The Celts were the Iron Age peoples of much of Europe / who in the Iron Age lived from Iberia and Ireland to the Danube
c. 800 BCE: Iron working spreads in central Europe and the Hallstatt culture begins

text: Most Celts were farmers who grew wheat and barley and kept cattle, pigs and sheep.
Rich rulers were buried with treasures, like a woman at Vix with a gold neck ring.
src: Most people were farmers who grew wheat and barley and kept cattle, pigs and sheep in farmsteads and villages

At Vix, a person of rank, usually identified as a woman, was buried ... with a gold torc and a giant Greek bronze krater / The Greek bronze krater, a vessel for mixing wine / gold torcs, the neck rings worn by nobles

text: Their priests, the druids, learned their lessons by heart instead of writing them down.
This silver cauldron shows a figure with antlers, often thought to be a Celtic god.
src: Caesar presents the druids as the priests and learned class of Gaul / they learned their lore by heart rather than writing it down
An antlered figure on the silver Gundestrup cauldron, found in a Danish bog in 1891 ... is commonly identified with Cernunnos

text: Celtic artists covered shields and neck rings with flowing curves, where faces and animals appear.
Some of these treasures were thrown into rivers and lakes as offerings to the gods.
src: turned them into flowing, asymmetrical curves in which faces and animals appear and dissolve / The finest works are in metal ... the Battersea Shield ... gold torcs
Archaeology shows offerings in water and in sanctuaries. Weapons, cauldrons and ornaments were thrown into lakes, rivers and bogs

text: Celtic warriors captured and robbed Rome, and some settled as far away as Asia Minor.
A king of Pergamon who beat them had statues made, like this dying Gaul.
src: in about 390 BCE a Gallic army under Brennus routed the Romans at the Allia and sacked Rome / three tribes crossed into Asia Minor ... and settled in the region later named Galatia
the victories of Attalus I of Pergamon over the Galatians were celebrated with statues such as the Dying Gaul

text: Later, Rome conquered most Celtic lands, though Vercingetorix led the Gauls against Julius Caesar.
Their art and place names remain, and Irish, Welsh and Breton are Celtic languages still spoken.
src: Rome conquered most Celtic lands from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE / Vercingetorix of the Arverni united most Gauls against him in 52 BCE
Rome conquered most of their lands, but their art, place names and languages endure / The Celtic languages still spoken are Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Welsh and Breton
